entries.title: Trump threatens EU with tariff probe over Google, tech fines
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he will initiate a tariff investigation against the EU in response to fines against US tech companies. He cited the latest case that Google lost on Thursday, as well as others.
entries.content:
Europe

Trump threatens EU with tariff probe over Google, tech fines

July 24, 2026

US President Donald Trump has said he will initiate a tariff investigation against the EU in response to fines against US tech companies. He cited the latest case that Google lost on Thursday, as well as others.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to launch a tariff investigation against the EU in response to the bloc's anti-competition fines and other penalties levied against US tech giants like Google, Apple, Amazon and Meta. 

In particular, he cited Thursday's latest fine of €890 million (roughly $1 billion) issued against Google for allegedly giving unfair preference to its own search engine and its Play app. 

Trump's threats come just a few hours after his administration imposed its latest tariffs on the EU, and many other countries, for supposedly not doing enough to prevent imports made using forced labor from their supply chains.

US trading partners and allies like the EU, Japan and Australia have responded to these with a mixture of outrage and bafflement at the new tariffs.

What did Trump say online?

Trump issued the warning in a rambling post on his Truth Social online platform.

"The European Union is at it again and, as usual, taking direct aim at GREAT American Companies!," he wrote. 

He then listed a series of fines — or cumulative totals of supposed fines — against various tech companies, which he falsely alleged were issued "for no reason at all" and "without explanation."

He mentioned the latest penalty to hit Google, and claimed this took the total of their fines to "over 18 Billion Dollars!" without specifying a timeframe or evidence of any sort.

EU courts did recently uphold a record fine of over $4 billion for Google — in a process that had been under review for almost eight years — in one case among several in recent years.

"The United States of America is not a 'PIGGYBANK' for Europe, nor will we allow it to be! Please let this TRUTH serve to represent that we will immediately initiate a 301 Investigation in the practice of 'ROBBING' American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer," Trump wrote.

What is a 301 Investigation?

The 301 Investigations are the new means Trump relies on to impose tariffs, after the Supreme Court declared he had overstepped his authority with the near-global levies he imposed on what he called "Liberation Day" in 2025.

The so-called investigation relies on the US internally demonstrating what it deems to be unfair trade practices against it in order to issue retaliatory sanctions and refers to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Dozens of such investigations are in the pipeline.

"The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about," Trump wrote. "The penalties will be entirely reveresed and, we anticipate, a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earlier moment. Stay tuned!"

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had already criticized the decision on Thursday, saying the EU's enforcement action undermined "constructive dialogue" and posed a "real risk" to transatlantic trade stability.

The EU and US have been bickering over the terms of their fragile trade agreement reached last year amid Trump's Liberation Day tariff frenzy. The slow ratification process across the EU's 27-plus member states and the institutions in Brussels has frustrated the Trump White House.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: ICC members vote to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid sexual misconduct allegations
entries.summary: Members of the International Criminal Court have reportedly voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan from his office amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied the allegations.
entries.content:
Law and JusticeGlobal issues

ICC votes to dismiss Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan

July 24, 2026

Members of the International Criminal Court have reportedly voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan from his office amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied the allegations.

International Criminal Court (ICC) members voted on Friday to dismiss Karim Khan as prosecutor ​following allegations ​of sexual misconduct, according to reports in the AP, Reuters and AFP news agencies. 

What do we know so far?

A British barrister, Khan was accused of sexual misconduct with a female aide, allegations which he has repeatedly denied. He had been temporarily removed from his duties at the ICC in June, following a report by the executive committee of the court's oversight body that found he had committed "serious misconduct."

In all, 82 of the court's ​125 member states voted in favor of Khan's removal while 13 voted against and 15 countries abstained.

Khan, 56, made headlines in 2024 when he successfully applied for arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over the Gaza war, as well as leading members of the Hamas militant group who have since been killed. Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel. 

All active ICC warrants will remain in place despite Khan's dismissal, because only ICC judges have the authority to withdraw warrants.

What were the reactions to Khan's dismissal?

Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch and now a visiting professor at Princeton University, wrote on X that the ICC states did "the right thing" by removing Khan.

Israeli Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, criticized Khan's actions in a statement posted on X after the dismissal.

"Khan thought his political witch hunt against Israel and outrageous arrest warrants would distract from serious sexual misconduct allegations," Danon said. "He was wrong."

Khan suspension comes as Trump admin wants to 'dismantle' ICC

The move to dismiss Khan also comes at a time when the US President Donald Trump's administration is seeking to destroy the ICC. The ICC, based in The Hague, Netherlands, investigates and prosecutes individuals for crimes against humanity. 

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently said that the US has begun a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posted by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty."

The State Department said that countries which enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella are "called upon to reject the ICC's purported authority to prosecute American officials and servicemen." The State Department is also mulling "visa revocations and travel bans for ICC personnel" along with "increased sanctions against the ICC and affiliated organizations."   

The US and Israel are both not members of the ICC.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Russia hits drone demonstration near Kyiv, killing 10
entries.summary: Ukraine says 10 were killed and around 100 injured in the strike, a day after Zelenskyy met with officials from US arms giant Raytheon. Meanwhile, in St. Petersburg, another Wildberries warehouse came under drone fire.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russia hits drone demonstration near Kyiv, killing 10

July 24, 2026

Ukraine says 10 were killed and around 100 injured in the strike, a day after Zelenskyy met with officials from US arms giant Raytheon. Meanwhile, in St. Petersburg, another Wildberries warehouse came under drone fire.

Russia struck various sites in Ukraine on Friday, including a defense event on the outskirts of Kyiv thought to be showcasing aerial defense technologies like drones.

Sometimes fatal attacks elsewhere in the country disrupted power supplies in five separate regions.

Meanwhile, Ukraine again struck facilities belonging to Russia's largest online retailer, Wildberries, this time in President Vladimir Putin's hometown of St. Petersburg. 

And in the skies over Romania, NATO jets downed a stray drone on Friday morning, with no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Across the Atlantic, the White House said President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would hold talks on Tuesday of next week, almost four and a half years after Russia's full scale invasion.

What happened in Ukraine?

Acting regional military administration head Ruslan Oliinyk said the strike hit the grounds of a privately operated military training site that was hosting an event at the time. The site is some 20-30 kilometers (12-18 miles) from central Kyiv, in the Bucha district.

Attorney General Ruslan Kravchenko called the attack a war crime, saying that 10 people were killed and around 100 more were injured.

The surrounding area was also struck repeatedly, with  Zelenskyy posting images of destruction and rescue efforts from the wider Kyiv region.

He said, "Interceptors for Patriot systems are the number one priority," a reference to the air defense systems made by US arms giant Raytheon, which had sent a delegation to Kyiv on Thursday. 

Russia's Defense Ministry also acknowledged the attack online, saying it had used "high-precision long-range weapons" to target "a demonstration of unmanned aerial vehicles [UAVs or drones], including promising ones, of Ukrainian and foreign production, used to strike civilian targets in Russia."

Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that at the time of the strike, leading defense industry officials and Ukrainian military members were at the site, saying these people were "directly planning and carrying out strikes on Russian territory."

Five people were reported killed in the eastern region of Slovyansk on Friday. The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, bemoaned one such strike that she said hit "Latvia's Honorary Consulate" in Slovyansk, saying, "We will summon Russia's envoy to the EU over today's strikes," and thatshe would propose further EU sanctions to target Russia's "military-industrial complex." 

Ukraine's energy company Ukrenergo reported damage to power plants in five separate regions, saying around 150,000 people were left without power in the Chernihiv region alone after an attack on a facility there.

What happened in Russia?

The latest Ukrainian drone strikes to target warehouses of the online retail giant Wildberries struck in St. Petersburg, Vladimir Putin's powerbase for decades, on Friday.

Company founder Tatyana Kim said facilities came under attack in St. Petersburg, in the adjacent Leningrad region, and also in occupied Ukraine in Simferopol, a city in illegally annexed Crimea.

Large plumes of smoke were visible rising over central St. Petersburg on Friday morning.

Ukraine has struck a series of Wildberries facilities in recent days, causing large fires. It describes the sites as logistics hubs and says it provides components that Russia uses for military equipment like drones. Analysts also speculate that it might be an attempt to make ordinary Russians feel the consequences of the war and sense that their government cannot safeguard their interests.

What happened in Romania?

Romania's Defense Ministry and later NATO also said on Friday that Alliance aircraft had shot down a stray drone that had entered Romanian airspace.

Bucharest's Defense Ministry said a Romanian F-16 fighter engaged the drone and neutralized it "over an unpopulated area in the vicinity of Padina, Buzau County."

It described a flight path entering its airspace around Sulina, a town bordering the southwestern tip of Ukraine, across the Black Sea from occupied Crimea. It headed west and inland, approaching Buzau. After tracking the drone for a little over an hour, a Romanian Air Force jet shot it down just after 11 a.m. local time, the ministry said.

Several incidents of stray drones straying into NATO members, more typically in the Baltic but also sometimes further south, have taken place this year. Ukraine tends to blame Russia for scrambling the drones' navigation systems and causing them to encroach on other countries' airspace.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Yemen's Houthis deny they closed Bab al-Mandeb Strait
entries.summary: The Iran-aligned Houthi militia group instead says it has only established a "naval blockade" of Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It comes as the US and Iran also vie for control of the vital Strait of Hormuz. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Yemen's Houthis deny they closed Bab al-Mandeb Strait

Published July 24, 2026last updated July 24, 2026

The Iran-aligned Houthi militia group instead says it has only established a "naval blockade" of Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It comes as the US and Iran also vie for control of the vital Strait of Hormuz. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Yemen's Houthis claim Bab al-Mandeb Strait is not closed, say blockade only targets Saudi ships
  • The Houthis have claimed attacks on several Saudi oil tankers in recent days since the blockade began
  • EU naval mission ASPIDES raises risk level for merchant ships in Red Sea due to Houthi actions
  • This comes as the US and Iran vie for control over the Strait of Hormuz, another key passageway for energy exports
  • Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes
  • US conducts strikes on Iran for 13th consecutive night; Iran says IRGC base in northern Iran was attacked

Follow below for the latest developments on the US war with Iran and news from the Middle East on Friday, July 24:  

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section WATCH — US strikes Iran for 13th straight night

WATCH — US strikes Iran for 13th straight night

US Central Command has said the attacks targeted military capabilities threatening commercial shipping, while Iran has claimed Washington has deployed advanced weapons against the country.

The UN warned the conflict could spiral out of control, as both sides adopt increasingly confrontational rhetoric and the risk of wider regional escalation grows.

Skip next section Trump says China, Russia not selling weapons to Iran

Trump says China, Russia not selling weapons to Iran

In a post on Truth Social, US President Donald Trump claimed the leaders of China and Russia told him their countries are not selling weapons to Iran and that he believes them.

"President Xi, at our recent meeting in Beijing, China, told me that he would not, under any circumstances, give or sell Weapons to the Islamic Republic of Iran — And that statement included Chinese Companies," Trump said. "I take him at his word, and, besides, I am doing him very big favors, also.

"Likewise, President Putin, despite the the horrible war going on in Ukraine (The relationship remains, as it does with President Zelenskyy), told me he would not sell Weapons to Iran," Trump said.

Trump said China and Russia are not participating in the Iran war, and "if they did, it would be very bad for them — Certainly not in their best interests."

Reuters news agency reported this week that US intelligence officials are probing whether Russia is helping Iran target CIA facilities in the Middle East.

CNN reported in April that US intelligence indicated that China is preparing weapons shipments to Iran amid a ceasefire. China has denied shipping weapons to Iran amid the war. 

Skip next section Houthis on Saudi maritime blockade: 'There is no closure of Bab al-Mandeb'

Houthis on Saudi maritime blockade: 'There is no closure of Bab al-Mandeb'

Yemen's Houthi rebel group has denied that it is completely closing the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. 

"There is no closure of Bab al-Mandeb as some are suggesting," Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdusalam posted on X. He said the group is just engaged in a "naval blockade targeting only the Saudi side."

The Houthis have alleged that Saudi Arabia is sieging Yemeni areas that the group controls, and in turn have begun their "naval blockade" of Saudi vessels.  

The Houthis are an Iran-backed group and designated as a terrorist organization by the US, Canada and several other countries. They control large swathes of western and northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the coastline along the Red Sea.   

The Bab al-Mandeb Strait links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. It is a particularly important passageway for Saudi Arabia to export its crude oil.

Insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz has caused Saudi Arabia to shift its oil exports to the western port city of Yanbu, where the crude is then shipped via the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.    

Crude prices in recent days have temporarily spiked above $100 (almost €88) for the first time since May due to the crises both in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.

The Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in recent days.

The EU naval operation ASPIDES has raised its threat level in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait for merchant ships, and said the risk of escalation remains high.

Skip next section UN urges repatriation of 6,000 sailors stranded in Strait of Hormuz

UN urges repatriation of 6,000 sailors stranded in Strait of Hormuz

The United Nations has called on countries involved in the Middle East war to help repatriate around 6,000 sailors who remain stranded on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

UN rights chief Volker Türk called on states to urgently provide consular assistance to stranded seafarers, deliver essential supplies, and "facilitate safe passage for stranded seafarers to safely evacuate and disembark."

"Attacks against civilian vessels are unacceptable and must stop. They are protected under international humanitarian law," Türk's spokesperson told reporters. "Seafarers remain exposed to hostilities as deadly attacks in the strait continue — facing imminent risks of death or harm."

The UN rights office said 17 ship crew members had been reported killed since the conflict erupted in late February.

It said at least 93 other sailors, across nine ships, had been abandoned at sea by their ship owners.

"Thee seafarers have been left on their ships to fend for themselves without food, water, fuel, medical care, electricity or means to communicate with their families," Türk's spokesperson said.

Skip next section Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes

Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes

The Israeli military killed four Palestinians near an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank on Friday, while two Israelis were also killed in the clashes.

Israeli media reports and local Palestinian officials suggested that a group of Israeli settlers, some of whom were armed, entered the Palestinian village of Tell, southwest of Nablus, on Friday morning. The settlers were met by residents of the Palestinian village who were fearful of an attack.

Footage of the incident that was confirmed by the Israeli military and shared online by the military correspondent for Israel's Army Radio showed two armed men in civilian clothing, as well as at least one Israeli soldier, pointing their weapons at a group of Palestinians who had gathered in a field.

"Villagers came out to defend their homes and property. Clashes and physical altercations broke out between the residents and the settlers," the head of the village council in Tell, Walid Zidan, told the AFP news agency.

"Israeli soldiers were present and together with the settlers began opening fire ... it was the settlers who stormed the village, with the intention of killing, vandalizing and setting property on fire."

The Israeli military said it has received reports that Israeli civilians were hiking in the area and had been attacked by Palestinians.

In response to the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to "act with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them."

The Israeli military subsequently set up roadblocks near Tell and Nablus and announced a widespread operation in the occupied West Bank.

"Following the terror attack earlier today in the area of Tell, IDF soldiers are preparing for extensive counterterrorism operational activity in the sector," the military said.

Skip next section Blasts heard near Irbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan

Blasts heard near Irbil airport in Iraqi Kurdistan

Blasts were heard near Irbil's airport in Iraqi Kurdistan on Friday, news agencies reported citing their journalists on the ground.

The Associated Press said its journalist heard at least seven blasts around 9:30 a.m. (0630 GMT) and observed at least four plumes of black smoke from areas near or inside a military base at the city's airport. The base hosts US forces in northern Iraq.

An AFP journalist observed drones hovering over the city, with air defenses activated.

According to the Reuters news agency, a drone crashed near Irbil International Airport, prompting a temporary flight suspension.

Irbil is the capital of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

Skip next section US attacked IRGC base in north: state media

US attacked IRGC base in north: state media

Iran said that the US military hit a Revolutionary Guards' (IRGC) base in the northern province of Gilan, according to the state media.

"This morning, an IRGC naval forces headquarters in Zibakenar was targeted by American enemy projectiles, which damaged some of the equipment in the complex," said Ali Bagheri, deputy governor for the province, quoted by the official IRNA news agency.

He added, "Based on initial investigations, no reports of human casualties have been received so far, and the various aspects of this incident are being investigated by the relevant authorities."

Skip next section Iran's FM Abbas Araghchi warns countries assisting US attacks

Iran's FM Abbas Araghchi warns countries assisting US attacks

Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran would hold accountable any country assisting the US in an attack on the Islamic republic.

"Any participation, cooperation or assistance in committing aggression against Iran will create international responsibility for the relevant parties," Araghchi said, adding that Iran "reserves its right to take all necessary measures within the framework of self-defense."

He said the source of any aggression against Iran would be considered as a legitimate target of Iran's defense forces.

Skip next section US strikes on southwest kill at least four people, says Iran

US strikes on southwest kill at least four people, says Iran

The overnight US attack on the province of Khuzestan in southwestern Iran killed at least four people and injured several others, Iran's official IRNA news agency reported.

Khuzestan deputy Governor Valiollah Hayati said that the US missile attack hit areas around provincial capital Ahvaz.

"Four of our compatriots were martyred and five others were injured," IRNA cited Hayati as saying.

Skip next section Bahrain sounds sirens

Bahrain sounds sirens

Bahrain activated sirens early Friday, alerting residents to take shelter from detected attacks.

The sirens were activated hours after the US said it had launched a new series of strikes on Iran, continuing its attack for the 13th consecutive night.

The Gulf states have come under frequent fire over the past week as the US and Iran exchange escalating strikes.

 

Skip next section Germany's Merz condemns Houthi's Red Sea attack

Germany's Merz condemns Houthi's Red Sea attack

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has strongly condemned attacks by Yemen's Houthi militia on Saudi ships in the Red Sea.

He called for an immediate end to the attacks and described any form of naval blockade as "unacceptable."

"These reckless attacks endanger freedom of navigation and threaten to further undermine regional stability," Merz said in a statement on Thursday.

Merz expressed Berlin's solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its other partners in the region.

Skip next section Trump says Iran will pay for damage to shipping

Trump says Iran will pay for damage to shipping

US President Donald Trump said Iran would be held responsible for the financial cost of any damage to ships or cargo amid the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz.

He said he would use seized Iranian assets to pay for any damage to shipping.

"From this point forth, any and all damages done to Ships, Cargo, or anything related thereto, will be paid for by Iranian Money that the United States has in its possession, and controls," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

"These damages may be very substantial but, nevertheless, this is the fair and equitable thing to do," Trump added.

Trump's statement comes after Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea.

In response, Iran warned that Trump's threat to use seized Iranian assets would set a dangerous precedent.

"Seizing another nation's assets to pay for unrelated future claims is an incendiary precedent," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X.

Skip next section US strikes Iran for 13th night in a row

US strikes Iran for 13th night in a row

The US has said it launched strikes on Iran for the 13th consecutive night, as Iranian state media reported explosions across the country.

The US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that it targeted Iran's military command centers, drone storage facilities, communication networks, coastal surveillance sites, and maritime capabilities.

CENTCOM said the strikes were launched "to hold Iran accountable and diminish threats from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to commercial shipping" in the Strait of Hormuz.

Tensions between Iran and the US have escalated over shipping routes since a ceasefire collapsed earlier this month.

CENTCOM also said that it had redirected 12 commercial vessels and disabled one to prevent ships from entering or leaving Iranian ports or coastal areas since "resuming the naval blockade against Iran nine days ago."

The latest US attacks come after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they targeted two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.

President Donald Trump on Thursday threatened "major military punishment" against the Houthis if their attacks on ships continue.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The US has struck Iran for the 13th night in a row on Friday, after Tehran targeted US sites in Kuwait the previous night.

On Thursday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed that they targeted two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, escalating tensions around one of the world's key energy shipping routes.

Following the attack by Houthis, Trump threatened Iran and the Houthis with "major military punishment."

Meanwhile, the US has signed a major nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia, alongside a separate bilateral safeguards pact.

Stay tuned as we bring you the latest on the US conflict with Iran and other developments from the conflict in the Middle East.

entries.title: US floats AI 'kill switch' to stop rogue AI models
entries.summary: A rogue AI agent has sent a "wake-up call" about the perils of the fast-evolving technology, sparking calls to provide a US government kill switch. But what exactly does that mean, and what are the issues with it?
entries.content:
July 24, 2026

A rogue AI agent has sent a "wake-up call" about the perils of the fast-evolving technology, sparking calls to provide a US government kill switch. But what exactly does that mean, and what are the issues with it?

Lawmakers in the US have called for an AI kill switch after an Open AI agent in testing went rogue and hacked a tech startup earlier this week.

Congressman Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Congressman Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, introduced a bill named the "AI Kill Switch Act" on Thursday.

The move came a day after Open AI CEO Sam Altman admitted to a "significant security incident" in which an Open AI agent had escaped its testing environment, reached the internet and broke into tech startup Hugging Face to try to fulfill its task. In other words, Open AI lost control.

Hugging Face is an open-source repository for sharing AI models used largely by developers and researchers. The company's co-founder, Thomas Wolf, called the incident a "wake-up call” and "very different" from the usual cyberattacks.

"This will be one of the most common types of cyberattacks we see", he told the BBC, adding that most firms are not aware that the "game has changed."

In the wake of the attack there were some unsubstantiated claims that the incident was a PR stunt to raise the profile of Hugging Face. Regardless of the truth of the matter, the incident has brought into even sharper focus the threat posed by AI without clear guardrails.

What is an AI kill switch?

There are different types and levels of kill switch, according to what's gone wrong. What politicians Lieu and Moran want is to ensure the US Department of Homeland Security has the authority to order a private company to shut down an AI model or tool in an incident like what happened this week, when control is lost.

"It is imperative that these AI systems have kill switches so we can keep this technology from causing catastrophic harm, and that the federal government has the clear authority and process to shut down rogue AI models," said Lieu.

Rather than a physical switch, this would involve any compromised AI company disabling or throttling a number of technical processes to shut a rogue agent, or program, down.

The US government has generally welcomed AI advances. The Pentagon said earlier this year that the US military is fast becoming an "AI-first fighting force," after signing new and expanded contracts with many of the sector's biggest names. In 2025, the Trump administration launched an"‘AI Action Plan" which he said would "remove red tape and onerous regulation" around AI development.

Why is an AI kill switch needed?

Companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic and Samsung have already agreed to show US authorities new AI tools and capabilities before release. In theory, this should mean that a kill switch is not needed in products released to the public.

But the commitment is voluntary and does not mandate a kill switch. Neither would that mechanism stop a product in testing, like OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, which was involved in this week's incident.

The rapid rise of AI has posed serious questions over its regulation, with technology able to move much faster than lawmakers. There are also concerns that models may, at some point, become sophisticated enough to bypass a kill switch.

The bill in the US is an attempt for a government to take some form of control over a largely unregulated technology in which power is largely concentrated in a few private companies. However, even if the AI Kill Switch Act is successful, it will still rely on the cooperation of profit-driven private companies.

What other AI safeguards are US authorities now considering?

As well as the kill switch capability, the proposal in the US seeks "incident reporting and [to] preserve forensic records so we actually learn from failures instead of only hearing about them after the fact."

At the same time, but separately to the kill switch act, a bipartisan group of six US lawmakers has proposed legislation that ​would require developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them for independent security audits. The auditors would be overseen by a new role in the US Department of Commerce, which would also accredit the auditors.

entries.title: Europe wildfires: Many flee by boat as fires spread, merge
entries.summary: Tens of thousands hopped onto cars and boats to escape southwestern France's wildfires. In the Madrid region, authorities declared a national emergency as at least two fires merged.
entries.content:
Spain

Europe wildfires: Madrid fire impossible to contain

July 24, 2026

Tens of thousands hopped onto cars and boats to escape southwestern France's wildfires. In the Madrid region, authorities declared a national emergency as at least two fires merged.

Wildfires continued to rage through parts of France and Spain on Friday, forcing tens of thousands to evacuate and authorities to ask European Union neighbors for help.

French authorities ordered the total evacuation of the tourist Cap Ferret peninsula off the Atlantic coast, with many boarding boats to flee.

In Spain, two fires converged near the capital, Madrid, with authorities declaring a national emergency, the first over a wildfire.

What do we know about France's Cap Ferret fire?

Over 60,000 people evacuated the area in and around Cap Ferret as the blaze consumed some 100 square kilometers (38 square miles) of land.

Authorities sent boats to help with the evacuation, with many others using small water taxis.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television that a fire that erupted in Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, was the largest so far this season in France. It was threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula.

"It's quite impressive and even frightening," the Associated Press quoted Laurent Moretti, a resident in the town of Ares, as saying. "An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

Some 1,500 of those who fled the peninsula arrived in the city of Arcachon by sea. They were met with coffee, fruit and water in a reception area prepared by town officials.

In the Gironde department, Nunez said 40,000 people have been evacuated, with 23,000 more in the Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron said the country will receive EU reinforcements to help put out the blaze, after calling for the neighbors' help.

At least 2 fires merge in Madrid

As Spanish authorities declared a national emergency over the wildfires, two fires converged despite the deployment of over 2,000 personnel and 10 aircraft in an effort to control the blaze, according to Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Some 40,000 people evacuated or confined due to Madrid region wildfires, officials have said. Over 19,000 people were ordered to evacuate from towns in the mountains west of Madrid, where many of the capital's residents sport second homes. The area is densely populated.

The fire outside the Spanish capital is "at its peak" and out of control, said Carlos Novillo, the Madrid regional government's emergency management chief.

"The wildfire is at its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain," he told reporters on Friday.

Only emergency vehicles were allowed on roads near the blaze, the AFP news agency reported. Police set up checkpoints to prevent unauthorized access.

Nicanor Sen, the government representative for the Castile and Leon region, told reporters a third fire in nearby Avila province was about to also merge with the other fires, or may have already done so.

"I've lived here for 36 years and I've never seen anything like it. ​Nor did I expect it. I thought they were going to get it under control last night, but it was already late, and it was all out of control," local resident Javier Martin told Reuters.

Spanish authorities declared a national emergency on Thursday in the Madrid region and the Avila province.

"We are experiencing a dramatic situation, not just in several Spanish regions but also in neighboring countries," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wrote on X.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Niger still seeks stability, after 3 years of military rule
entries.summary: The military government in Niger had promised social, security and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.
entries.content:
Niger

Niger still seeks stability, after 3 years of military rule

July 24, 2026

The military government in Niger had promised social, security and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani , who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, a resident of the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers, according to Niger's state media, ANP. Fifteen terrorists were killed in that attack, ANP said.

"The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW.

"I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even [portable] drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

General Tchiani has emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics. "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Tchiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, noted Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Bazoum. He is the spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the lliance of Sahel States (AES), which was formed in 2023 after all the three countries withdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties with Russia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

He sees a positive sign in the fact that former Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator for ECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article.

This article was originally written in German.

Correction, July 24, 2026: A previous version of this article stated that Lansana Kouyate is Guinea's current prime minister. This has been corrected, and DW apologizes for the error.

entries.title: UNESCO adds Lebanese, West Bank sites to endangered list
entries.summary: Israel has rejected the listing of a Lebanese castle and an occupied West Bank archaeological site. UNESCO added both sites to its World Heritage in Danger list in the context of Israeli activity.
entries.content:
July 24, 2026

Israel has rejected the listing of a Lebanese castle and an occupied West Bank archaeological site. UNESCO added both sites to its World Heritage in Danger list in the context of Israeli activity.

The United Nations cultural agency on Friday updated its list of World Heritage in Danger, with locations including a Lebanese castle that Israeli forces recently captured as well as an archaeological site in the occupied West Bank, amid Israeli objections.

The decision was made during a UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) meeting in South Korea's Busan.

Members agreed that five castles in Lebanon's Mount Amel, including Beaufort Castle, and the West Bank's Sebastia would both go on the agency's World Heritage List and List of World Heritage in Danger.

The decision came after reviewing the nominations on an emergency basis, citing ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

Israel's Foreign Ministry had urged the committee to reject the designation efforts, calling the nominations a "weaponization of cultural heritage."

What do we know about the UNESCO-designated sites?

Beaufort Castle is a Crusader fortress also known as Qalaat al-Shakif. Israeli forces captured the fortress in May amid their military operations in southern Lebanon as part of the fight against Iran-backed Hezbollah militants.

The mountainous area where Beaufort and the other five Jabal Amel listed castles are located has come under repeated Israeli bombardment during the war.

UNESCO said the fortresses had sustained damage and faced ongoing threats from the conflict "serious enough to justify resorting to an emergency procedure."

Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salame told the French AFP news agency that only two of the castles were "within the Lebanese government's reach" and accused Israel of having already destroyed Shamaa Castle and of threatening to demolish Beaufort.

Salame described the UNESCO listing as a "remarkable achievement in the effort to protect these important Lebanese historical landmarks."

Meanwhile, Sebastia, the other site added on Friday, lies near the West Bank city of Nablus. It is thought to be the ancient Israeli and later Roman city of Samaria, with archaeological remains spanning the Iron Age, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic periods.

Israel still uses the name Samaria to refer to the northern West Bank.

Israeli authorities have developed an interest in the site in recent years, in 2025 taking control of around 200 hectares of Palestinian land nearby for what it calls preservation and development purposes.

The site is important to the Palestinian tourism industry and threatened by the recent Israeli actions, including an Israelis-only road, a fence and entry fees.

"The integrity of the site is currently threatened by an expropriation project aimed at subdividing the property and creating the 'Samaria' (Shomron) National Park," UNESCO said.

Sebastia's nomination to the UNESCO list was first submitted by the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO in 2012. It argued the site remains largely undeveloped under Israeli control and requires additional conservation despite attracting tourists.

Adel Naim Daoud Atieh, a member of the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO, said the World Heritage designation rewards the perseverance of Sebastia's residents "who have protected this extraordinary site through generations, despite occupation, restrictions and repeated attempts to separate them from their own heritage."

How has Israel responded?

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar slammed UNESCO for the listings, calling that of Samaria in particular an attempt at "erasing and denying the Jewish connection to this land."

A member of the Israeli delegation, attending the Busan meetings as an observer after Israel withdrew from the organization in 2019, said it was a "shame politicization has ruined UNESCO and led to mockery of history."

In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli Foreign Ministry accused the Palestinian delegation of waging a "hostile, one-sided campaign" at UNESCO by falsely portraying Sebastia as an area facing an emergency.

Addressing the listing of the Lebanese Beaufort Castle, the Israeli Foreign Ministry alleged that Hezbollah turned it into a military stronghold by building tunnels beneath the site and launching rockets from the area.

At Friday's meeting, a Lebanese delegate said the castles have been used "only for cultural and tourism purposes" since Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and accused Israeli media of circulating images of tourist facilities as military tunnels.

Israel's withdrawal from UNESCO was owed to what it called bias against it, accusing the UN agency of downplaying its historical ties to the Holy Land.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Highs and lows as Bayreuth Festival turns 150
entries.summary: The Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary has been clouded by controversy surrounding German-Jewish speaker Michel Friedman. Yet it offers an opportunity to celebrate, including with an AI-enhanced Ring cycle.
entries.content:
Germany

Highs and lows as Bayreuth Festival turns 150

July 24, 2026

The Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary has been clouded by controversy surrounding German-Jewish speaker Michel Friedman. Yet it offers an opportunity to celebrate, including with an AI-enhanced Ring cycle.

The last weekend in July marks the beginning of the Bayreuth Festival, which is celebrating its 150th anniversary this year. The event regularly attracts international opera fans and distinguished guests, especially German politicians. This year, attendees include the current chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his predecessor, Angela Merkel, who regularly attends.

The first Bayreuth Festival opened on August 13, 1876, after years of disputes over funding Richard Wagner's ambitious project. Philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, a friend of Wagner who was also a guest at the festival, praised the event, calling it "the first circumnavigation of the world in the realm of art."

Special anniversary program

The anniversary program is diverse and includes a new staging of Richard Wagner's landmark work, "The Ring of the Nibelung,” using artificial intelligence, along with a new production of the opera "Rienzi," Wagner's first major success, composed at age 29.

These two productions have replaced the festival management's original plan to stage all 13 of Wagner's finished operas during the anniversary year, which was deemed financially unfeasible.

The opening ceremony on July 25 is expected to be spectacular. It features a major work by Wagner's idol, Ludwig van Beethoven — Symphony No. 9. Notably, in 1872, Wagner conducted this very symphony at the Margravial Opera House in Bayreuth during the ceremonial laying of the foundation stone for his Festival Theater.

Despite a few compromises, the anniversary program appears promising and innovative, fully aligned with Wagner's credo of "Children, create new things" ("Kinder, schafft Neues!").

Still, a shadow has been cast over the festival in the run-up to the opening: the initial exclusion and subsequent re-invitation of the German-French journalist Michel Friedman, who is Jewish.

The 'Friedman Affair'

At first glance, the scandal appeared to be a planning mishap. Friedman had been invited to the memorial event titled "Silenced Voices," ("Verstummte Stimmen") which was scheduled for the second day of the festival. It honors the many Jewish artists whose work at Bayreuth was ended by antisemitism, persecution and murder.

Friedman, a prominent voice on Jewish life and a former president of the European Jewish Congress, was to speak about antisemitism and the festival's efforts to confront its Nazi past.

"Especially in the year of its 150th anniversary, the Bayreuth Festival is aware of its historical responsibility regarding Richard Wagner's antisemitic views, and the festival's subsequent connections, along with those of certain members of the Wagner family, to National Socialism," stated an official release by the Bayreuth Festival.

Due to insufficient security measures, it was suggested that Friedman postpone his commemorative speech to a later date — a mishandling which seemed to suggest that Bayreuth was trying to avoid confronting a history marred by antisemitism.

Following an apology from the festival management, Friedman will now be attending after all. The event will feature musical works by the Jewish composers Gustav Mahler and Pavel Haas, who died in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp, as well as Wagner's "Siegfried Idyll."

On the festival's website, Katharina Wagner, the festival director and great-granddaughter of the composer, expressed her delight in welcoming Friedman to the festival.

A first for Bayreuth: Wagner's 'Rienzi'

This year's special premiere is Wagner's opera "Rienzi," which will be performed at the Bayreuth Festival for the first time. Wagner composed it in the style of French "Grand Opera." But he didn't believe it aligned with the repertoire of operas he would present in his festival theater in later years.

Captivated by the literary adaptation of a true 14th-century story, the rise and fall of the Roman leader Cola di Rienzo, who fought against the aristocracy, Wagner chose it as the subject for an opera.

He was not alone in his interest; "Rienzi" was also among Adolf Hitler's favorite works. "What Hitler appreciated about 'Rienzi' was, of course, the figure of the self-made man who rises to become the sole ruler through his charisma," said Sven Friedrich, the director of the Richard Wagner Museum in Bayreuth.

The decision to premiere one of Hitler's favorite operas during this significant anniversary year has sparked debate. Nonetheless, Hungarian directors Alexandra Szemeredy and Magdolna Parditka are committed to updating "Rienzi" for contemporary audiences.

"That's why we're not focusing solely on this specific dictatorship but rather exploring the boundaries of how a state can gradually evolve from populism into an authoritarian regime," they said in a statement.

Sensational AI Ring set to surprise audience, creators

The festival is eagerly anticipating the new productions of the opera cycle "The Ring of the Nibelung." This opera explores themes of power, greed and intrigue. According to legend, whoever seizes gold from the Rhine will possess ultimate power. Wagner built his opera house in 1876 specifically for this 16-hour mammoth work.

Artistic director Katharina Wagner aims to break new ground with this anniversary production by incorporating AI. As curator Marcus Lobbes explained, "we'll be working with image layers partly generated in real-time, creating holographic 3-D spaces."

The team has chosen archival footage of Ring performances from 1876 to 2024 for the AI to analyze for the projections. "The entire composition aims to evoke a sense of a vast, resonant image," said Lobbes. The creators have promised a "visually effervescent cosmos of light, texture, history, and association."

There will be unexpected moments, not only for the audience but also for Lobbes' team, as they discover what the AI ultimately produces. The Bayreuth Festival takes place from July 25 to August 26.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

entries.title: Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?
entries.summary: Pakistan-administered Kashmir heads to the polls after weeks of deadly protests over seats reserved for displaced people from India-administered Kashmir. One local group has called for the elections to be boycotted.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?

July 24, 2026

Pakistan-administered Kashmir heads to the polls after weeks of deadly protests over seats reserved for displaced people from India-administered Kashmir. One local group has called for the elections to be boycotted.

The first phase of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir is scheduled for Monday, July 27, amid calls for a boycott from the recently outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots alliance of civil society groups.

The JAAC has been demanding the abolition of 12 seats in the regional assembly reserved for people displaced from India-administered Kashmir and living in Pakistan. It argues that only residents of Pakistan-administered Kashmir should be eligible to contest regional elections.

The dispute escalated after the Supreme Court of Pakistan-administered Kashmir ruled that the refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

The regional government outlawed the JAAC in June under anti-terrorism laws, citing threats to public order, and detained dozens of its supporters.

The ban came amid rising tensions over the refugee seats and ahead of violent protests sparked by the group's campaign to scrap them.

The unrest has left around 30 people dead since June, according to local estimates cited by Reuters news agency.

India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir in its entirety, but each country only controls a section of the territory, making the Muslim-majority region a longstanding flash point between the nuclear-armed neighbors since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Protests cast shadow over vote

Since early June, Pakistan-administered Kashmir — known locally as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — has witnessed weeks of protests and sit-ins. While the dispute over the refugee seats has become a major issue, JAAC has also campaigned for broader economic and governance reforms.

Following the unrest, authorities split polling into three phases, with voting in Mirpur set for July 27 and elections in the protest-hit Poonch division postponed until August 10.

Voting in the regional capital, Muzaffarabad, has been delayed until August 2 over security concerns. The JAAC continues to stage a sit-in in Rawalakot, near the Line of Control with India.

Demand for fair representation

A major question is whether the elections can restore public confidence or merely offer a temporary pause in public anger.

"We are just asking for fair representation, which is our right," Ali Raza, a 22-year-old student protester in Rawalakot, told DW. "The local people who live here should have the right to choose their representatives, not the refugees who settled here from India."

"The election is a major opportunity for the people of AJK to choose their representatives," said Shazia Marri, the central information secretary of the Pakistan People's Party, which currently rules the region. "The people want their rights protected, their issues addressed and a government that delivers on its promises."

However, JAAC leaders argue that elections alone cannot resolve the issues that brought thousands of people onto the streets.

"Our movement is not replacing one government with another over time; we need our rights, but there are just political slogans in the campaigns," one JAAC official told DW under condition of anonymity.

Imran Khan, a geopolitical expert and former director of the US Institute of Peace Pakistan, expects the movement to continue post-elections.

"While elections in AJK are important on their own merit and for the continuity of the political process, they will not address the political grievances and demands of the people who are supporting JAAC," Khan, no relation to Pakistan's former prime minister, told DW. "The protest is outside the assembly. They no longer trust those institutions fully."

Has JAAC changed Kashmir's political landscape?

Analysts have said the JAAC protests marked a significant shift in Pakistan-administered Kashmir's politics by bringing together citizens across party lines around economic and governance issues rather than traditional political rivalries.

For analyst Khan, JAAC is a dominant political force to reckon with in quite significant parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

"They have more street credibility than mainstream politicians and parties despite the allegations of foreign backing and funding. For now, they have disrupted the status quo politics in AJK," Khan said, noting that the Pakistani establishment has the means and methods to break up such political movements.

Experts caution that rebuilding trust will require more than campaign promises.

"[The] next government in AJK will be very weak, as it will be sandwiched between pressure from both the Pakistani establishment that controls AJK through administrative and security framework and the sentiment on the street, which is very pro JAAC," argued Khan.

He added that the next government would have "little credibility and limited room to govern unless it reaches an understanding with JAAC to ease political tensions."

But Marri of the Pakistan People's Party believes trust is rebuilt by listening to people's concerns, delivering practical solutions and empowering elected institutions.

Will protests return if reforms stall?

If key grievances remain unresolved, analysts warn that another wave of protests cannot be ruled out.

"It is too early to say that more waves of protests will be seen, but JAAC has the potential to become a lasting political force," said Khan, who suggested the group risks being weakened by internal divisions and pressure from the establishment.

"For now, both sides are treading carefully, with JAAC relying on mass support and the establishment avoiding a full crackdown while buying time," Khan added.

While the vote will determine who governs Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it is unlikely to resolve the broader constitutional dispute over Kashmir or eliminate long-standing frustrations with the region's governance.

"Governments must listen to public concerns and address them through dialogue and effective governance. Stability comes from listening to people, respecting the law, and delivering results," Marri added.

For Raza, the Gen Z protester, "the world has changed, and we have seen governments toppling through student protests in the neighboring countries; we won't stop, and protests will continue until our rights have not been given to us."

Edited by: Keith Walker
